s.line: For three days Dorothy heard nothing from Oz.
s.note: בְּמֶשֶׁךְ + a stretch of time = "for / during": בְּמֶשֶׁךְ הַיּוֹם (during the day), בְּמֶשֶׁךְ שָׁנִים (for years). The noun מֶשֶׁךְ (duration) has the same root as נִמְשַׁךְ (lasted).

s.line: These were sad days for the little girl, although her friends were all quite happy and contented.
s.note: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ = although. In everyday speech you will hear לַמְרוֹת שֶׁ more often; both are correct. מְרֻצֶּה (satisfied, content) is a pu'al participle like מְאֻשָּׁר: literally "made content". לָקוֹחַ מְרֻצֶּה = a satisfied customer.

s.line: The Scarecrow told them there were wonderful thoughts in his head;
s.note: שֶׁיֵּשׁ: in reported speech Hebrew keeps the tense of the original words. He said "there are thoughts in my head", so Hebrew says שֶׁיֵּשׁ (present), where English shifts to "there were".

s.line: but he would not say what they were because he knew no one could understand them but himself.
s.note: לֹא הִסְכִּים + infinitive = "would not, refused to". הֵן and אוֹתָן are feminine because מַחֲשָׁבָה is feminine. חוּץ מִמֶּנּוּ = "except him": מִן with endings gives מִמֶּנִּי, מִמְּךָ, מִמֶּנּוּ, מִמֶּנָּה.

s.line: When the Tin Woodman walked about he felt his heart rattling around in his breast;
s.note: הִסְתּוֹבֵב = to turn around, and also to wander about: הִסְתּוֹבַבְנוּ בָּעִיר (we walked around town). קִשְׁקֵשׁ = to rattle; in everyday speech it mostly means "to talk nonsense" or "to scribble": אַל תְּקַשְׁקֵשׁ! (stop talking nonsense!), קִשְׁקוּשִׁים (scribbles, nonsense).

w: שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ|that he had|~lit. that was to him
s.line: and he told Dorothy he had discovered it to be a kinder and more tender heart than the one he had owned when he was made of flesh.

w: מִשּׁוּם דָּבָר|of anything|~with לֹא: of nothing
s.line: The Lion declared he was afraid of nothing on earth,
s.note: הִכְרִיז = declared, announced. It is a news word: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה הִכְרִיזָה עַל … (the government announced …), הַכְרָזָה (a declaration, an announcement). Note פָּחַד מִ־: you are afraid from something.

s.line: and would gladly face an army or a dozen of the fierce Kalidahs.
s.note: לְהִתְמוֹדֵד עִם = to face, to cope with. You will hear it constantly: לְהִתְמוֹדֵד עִם לַחַץ (to cope with stress), הִתְמוֹדְדוּת (coping). תְּרֵיסַר = a dozen.

s.line: Thus each of the little party was satisfied except Dorothy, who longed more than ever to get back to Kansas.
s.note: יוֹתֵר מִתָּמִיד = "more than ever", literally "more than always". חֲבוּרָה = a group of friends, a gang (in the friendly sense), from the same root as חָבֵר.

s.line: On the fourth day, to her great joy, Oz sent for her,
s.note: לְשִׂמְחָתָהּ = "to her joy". This pattern, לְ + feeling + possessive ending, is very common: לְהַפְתָּעָתִי (to my surprise), לְצַעֲרִי (unfortunately, lit. to my sorrow), לְמַזָּלֵנוּ (luckily for us).

w: קִבֵּל אֶת פָּנֶיהָ|greeted her|~idiom: lit. received her face (pi'el · ק־ב־ל)
s.line: and when she entered the Throne Room he greeted her pleasantly:
s.note: קִבֵּל אֶת פָּנֶיהָ = "he received her face", i.e. welcomed her. The noun is קַבָּלַת פָּנִים, a reception or welcome (for guests, or at a wedding before the ceremony).

s.line: “Sit down, my dear;
s.note: יַקִּירָתִי = "my dear" to a woman or girl; to a man it is יַקִּירִי. יָקָר = dear, and also expensive.

s.line: I think I have found the way to get you out of this country.”
s.note: יָצָא (pa'al) = to go out; הוֹצִיא (hif'il) = to take out, make go out. This pa'al/hif'il pair ("do" / "cause to do") is one of the most useful patterns in Hebrew.

s.line: “And back to Kansas?” she asked eagerly.
s.note: בְּהִתְלַהֲבוּת = with enthusiasm. מִתְלַהֵב = excited, enthusiastic; לֶהָבָה = a flame. Note בַּחֲזָרָה = back, in return: לָתֵת בַּחֲזָרָה (to give back).

w: אֵין לִי שֶׁמֶץ שֶׁל מֻשָּׂג|I haven’t the faintest notion|~idiom: lit. I have no trace of a notion
s.line: “Well, I’m not sure about Kansas,” said Oz, “for I haven’t the faintest notion which way it lies.
s.note: אֵין לִי שֶׁמֶץ שֶׁל מֻשָּׂג = "I haven't the faintest idea". The everyday short form is אֵין לִי מֻשָּׂג. לְגַבֵּי = regarding, about: מָה לְגַבֵּי מָחָר? (what about tomorrow?).

s.line: But the first thing to do is to cross the desert,
and then it should be easy to find your way home.”
s.note: אָמוּר is the pa'ul participle of אָמַר, literally "said", but it is the everyday word for "supposed to": הוּא אָמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ בְּשֶׁבַע (he's supposed to arrive at seven). הַבַּיְתָה = homeward; the ending ה means "to".

s.line: “How can I cross the desert?” she inquired.
“Well, I’ll tell you what I think,” said the little man.
s.note: אַגִּיד: in everyday Hebrew the future of "say, tell" usually comes from לְהַגִּיד (hif'il): אַגִּיד, תַּגִּיד, נַגִּיד. תַּגִּיד לִי = tell me; נַגִּיד also means "let's say".

s.line: “You see, when I came to this country it was in a balloon.
s.note: כַּדּוּר פּוֹרֵחַ = a hot-air balloon, literally "a flying ball". פָּרַח usually means "to bloom" (פֶּרַח = a flower), but it also has an older meaning "to fly off", kept in phrases like זֶה פָּרַח לִי מֵהָרֹאשׁ (it slipped my mind).

s.line: You also came through the air, being carried by a cyclone.
So I believe the best way to get across the desert will be through the air.
s.note: הַטּוֹבָה בְּיוֹתֵר = the best. בְּיוֹתֵר after the adjective is the standard written superlative; in speech you will mostly hear הֲכִי before it: הַדֶּרֶךְ הֲכִי טוֹבָה.

s.line: Now, it is quite beyond my powers to make a cyclone;
s.note: מֵעֵבֶר לְ = beyond, on the other side of: מֵעֵבֶר לַיָּם (overseas), זֶה מֵעֵבֶר לְכֹחוֹתַי (it's beyond me). לְיַצֵּר = to produce, manufacture; יַצְרָן = a manufacturer.

s.line: but I’ve been thinking the matter over, and I believe I can make a balloon.”
“How?” asked Dorothy.
“A balloon,” said Oz, “is made of silk, which is coated with glue to keep the gas in it.
s.note: מְצֻפֶּה is the pu'al (passive) participle of צִפָּה (pi'el), "to coat": עוּגִיּוֹת מְצֻפּוֹת שׁוֹקוֹלָד (chocolate-coated cookies). Without vowels צִפָּה is also the pi'el "to expect": לֹא צִפִּיתִי לָזֶה (I didn't expect that).

w: יֵשׁ לִי|I have|~lit. there is to me
s.line: I have plenty of silk in the Palace, so it will be no trouble to make the balloon.
s.note: לֹא תִּהְיֶה שׁוּם בְּעָיָה = "there will be no problem", the future of the everyday אֵין בְּעָיָה (no problem, sure). The verb is feminine, תִּהְיֶה, to agree with בְּעָיָה.

s.line: But in all this country there is no gas to fill the balloon with, to make it float.”
s.note: רִחֵף = to float or hover in the air. From the same root: רַחְפָן, the modern word for a drone. כְּדֵי שֶׁ + future = "so that".

s.line: “If it won’t float,” remarked Dorothy, “it will be of no use to us.”
s.note: הוֹעִיל = to be of use, to help. זֶה לֹא יוֹעִיל = it won't help; תּוֹעֶלֶת = benefit, use. הֵעִיר (remarked) is the same verb as "woke someone up"; the context tells you which.

s.line: “True,” answered Oz.
“But there is another way to make it float, which is to fill it with hot air.
s.note: גָּרַם לְ… + infinitive = to make someone or something do: הוּא גָּרַם לִי לִצְחֹק (he made me laugh). With a noun it means "to cause", a news favorite: הַסּוּפָה גָּרְמָה נֵזֶק (the storm caused damage).

w: נֵלֵךְ לְאִבּוּד|will be lost|~idiom: lit. go to loss (pa'al · ה־ל־ך)
s.line: Hot air isn’t as good as gas, for if the air should get cold the balloon would come down in the desert, and we should be lost.”
s.note: הָלַךְ לְאִבּוּד = to get lost (a person, or a thing: הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת הָלְכוּ לְאִבּוּד). הִתְקָרֵר = to get cold, and also to catch a cold: אֲנִי מְקֻרָר (I have a cold).

s.line: “We!” exclaimed the girl.
“Are you going with me?”
s.note: נָסַע = to go by vehicle, to travel; הָלַךְ is to go on foot. אִתִּי = with me (אִתְּךָ, אִתָּךְ, אִתּוֹ, אִתָּהּ).

s.line: “Yes, of course,” replied Oz.
s.note: הֵשִׁיב = replied, a slightly more formal word than עָנָה. It is the hif'il of שָׁב (return), so literally "returned (an answer)". In news: הַמִּשְׂרָד הֵשִׁיב כִּי … (the ministry replied that …).

s.line: “I am tired of being such a humbug.
If I should go out of this Palace my people would soon discover I am not a Wizard,
and then they would be vexed with me for having deceived them.
s.note: רִמָּה = to deceive, cheat: the same root as רַמַּאי (humbug, cheat) just above, and רַמָּאוּת (fraud). כָּעַס עַל = to be angry at someone, and עַל שֶׁ… gives the reason.

s.line: So I have to stay shut up in these rooms all day, and it gets tiresome.
s.note: נַעֲשָׂה (nif'al of עָשָׂה) = to become: נַעֲשָׂה קַר (it got cold). It can also be passive, "was done", so the context decides. מְשַׁעֲמֵם = boring; מְשֻׁעֲמָם (pu'al) = bored, the person who is bored.

s.line: I’d much rather go back to Kansas with you and be in a circus again.”
s.note: הָיִיתִי + participle = "I would …", the usual conditional: הָיִיתִי מַעֲדִיף (I'd prefer), הָיִיתִי בָּא (I'd come). הוֹפִיעַ = to appear, and also to perform on stage; הוֹפָעָה = a show, a concert.

s.line: “I shall be glad to have your company,” said Dorothy.
s.note: אֶשְׂמַח = "I'd be glad", a polite everyday formula: אֶשְׂמַח לַעֲזֹר (I'd be happy to help), נִשְׂמַח לִרְאוֹת אֶתְכֶם (we'd love to see you).

s.line: “Thank you,” he answered.
“Now, if you will help me sew the silk together, we will begin to work on our balloon.”
s.note: עָזַר לְ: in Hebrew you help to someone, so תַּעַזְרִי לִי, never אוֹתִי. תְּפִירָה = sewing; תּוֹפֶרֶת = a seamstress.

s.line: So Dorothy took a needle and thread,
and as fast as Oz cut the strips of silk into proper shape the girl sewed them neatly together.
s.note: גָּזַר = to cut out (with scissors). Without vowels it is spelled like גֶּזֶר (carrot), and גְּזַר דִּין is a court sentence. מְסֻדָּר (pu'al, "arranged") = neat, tidy: חֶדֶר מְסֻדָּר (a tidy room).

s.line: First there was a strip of light green silk, then a strip of dark green and then a strip of emerald green;
s.note: יָרֹק בָּהִיר / יָרֹק כֵּהֶה = light / dark green; the color comes first and בָּהִיר or כֵּהֶה follows it. All the words agree in gender: מֶשִׁי יָרֹק (masc.), רְצוּעָה יְרֻקָּה כֵּהָה (fem.).

w: לְאוֹז בָּא|Oz felt like|~idiom: lit. (it) came to Oz
s.line: for Oz had a fancy to make the balloon in different shades of the color about them.
s.note: בָּא לִי = "I feel like (doing)", one of the most common phrases in spoken Hebrew: בָּא לִי גְּלִידָה (I feel like ice cream), לֹא בָּא לִי (I don't feel like it). גָּוֶן, plural גְּוָנִים = a shade or tone of a color.

s.line: It took three days to sew all the strips together,

w: הָיָה לָהֶם|they had|~lit. there was to them
s.line: but when it was finished they had a big bag of green silk more than twenty feet long.
s.note: הִסְתַּיֵּם = to end, be finished (hitpa'el); the pi'el סִיֵּם = to finish something: סִיַּמְתִּי אֶת הָעֲבוֹדָה → הָעֲבוֹדָה הִסְתַּיְּמָה. Baum's twenty feet is about six meters.

s.line: Then Oz painted it on the inside with a coat of thin glue, to make it airtight,
s.note: מָרַח = to spread or smear: לִמְרֹחַ חֶמְאָה עַל לֶחֶם (to spread butter on bread). אָטוּם = sealed, airtight or watertight. Said of a person it means insensitive or dense: הוּא כָּל כָּךְ אָטוּם.

s.line: after which he announced that the balloon was ready.
s.note: מוּכָן (ready) is the hof'al participle of הֵכִין (hif'il, to prepare): literally "prepared". The same hif'il/hof'al pair as הִזְמִין (invited) → מוּזְמָן (invited guest). הוֹדִיעַ = to announce, inform; הוֹדָעָה = a message, also a text message.

s.line: “But we must have a basket to ride in,” he said.

w: הַחַיָּל עִם הַזָּקָן הַיָּרֹק|the soldier with the green whiskers
s.line: So he sent the soldier with the green whiskers for a big clothes basket,
s.note: לְהָבִיא (hif'il of בָּא, come) = to bring, literally "to make come". סַל כְּבִיסָה = a laundry basket; כְּבִיסָה is both the washing and the laundry itself.

s.line: which he fastened with many ropes to the bottom of the balloon.
s.note: קָשַׁר = to tie. The noun קֶשֶׁר = a knot, but mostly "contact, connection": לִיצֹר קֶשֶׁר (to get in touch), בְּקֶשֶׁר לְ… (regarding …). Putting the object first (אֶת הַסַּל הוּא קָשַׁר) stresses it: "the basket, he tied …".

s.line: When it was all ready, Oz sent word to his people that he was going to make a visit to a great brother Wizard who lived in the clouds.
s.note: עוֹמֵד לְ… + infinitive = "is about to", literally "stands to": הָרַכֶּבֶת עוֹמֶדֶת לָצֵאת (the train is about to leave). Very common in the news: הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה עוֹמֶדֶת לְהַחְלִיט. בִּקֵּר אֵצֶל = to visit someone at their place. עָמִית = a colleague, a fellow professional.

s.line: The news spread rapidly throughout the city
s.note: הִתְפַּשֵּׁט = to spread (news, fire, a disease); the same verb also means "to undress". יְדִיעָה = a news item, from יָדַע (know); the newspaper יְדִיעוֹת אַחֲרוֹנוֹת is "latest news".

s.line: and everyone came to see the wonderful sight.
Oz ordered the balloon carried out in front of the Palace,
s.note: צִוָּה = to order, command; the same root gives מִצְוָה (a commandment, a good deed) and צֶוֶת (a team, crew). English "ordered the balloon carried" becomes an infinitive in Hebrew: צִוָּה לְהוֹצִיא, "ordered to take out".

s.line: and the people gazed upon it with much curiosity.
s.note: הִבִּיט בְּ = to look at; the preposition is בְּ, so הִבִּיטוּ בּוֹ. סַקְרָן = curious, סַקְרָנוּת = curiosity.

s.line: The Tin Woodman had chopped a big pile of wood,
s.note: Hebrew has no separate pluperfect ("had chopped"); the plain past is used, and כְּבָר (already) shows that it happened earlier. חָטַב = to chop wood, as in חוֹטֵב עֵצִים.

s.line: and now he made a fire of it,
and Oz held the bottom of the balloon over the fire so that the hot air that arose from it would be caught in the silken bag.
s.note: יִתָּפֵס is the nif'al future of תָּפַס (catch): "will be caught". The nif'al swallows the נ into a dagesh in the future: יִתָּפֵס, יִכָּנֵס. מְדוּרָה = a bonfire, campfire; מִמֶּנָּה is feminine because אֵשׁ is feminine.

s.line: Gradually the balloon swelled out and rose into the air, until finally the basket just touched the ground.
s.note: הִתְנַפֵּחַ = to swell, inflate (itself); נִפֵּחַ (pi'el) = to blow up something, like a balloon or a tire. נָגַע בְּ = to touch, with בְּ. בְּקֹשִׁי = barely, hardly.

w: בְּקוֹל רָם|in a loud voice|~fixed phrase
s.line: Then Oz got into the basket and said to all the people in a loud voice:
s.note: בְּקוֹל רָם = aloud, in a loud voice: לִקְרֹא בְּקוֹל רָם (to read aloud). רָם = high, lofty.

s.line: “I am now going away to make a visit.
While I am gone the Scarecrow will rule over you.
s.note: כָּל עוֹד = as long as, while: כָּל עוֹד אַתָּה כָּאן (as long as you're here). מָלַךְ עַל = to reign over; מֶלֶךְ, מַלְכָּה and מַמְלָכָה share the root.

s.line: I command you to obey him as you would me.”
s.note: צִוָּה עַל (command) and צִיֵּת לְ (obey) sound alike but have different roots: צ־ו־ה and צ־י־ת. מְצַיֵּת = obedient. Note the prepositions: you command עַל someone, you obey לְ someone.

s.line: The balloon was by this time tugging hard at the rope that held it to the ground, for the air within it was hot,
s.note: מָשַׁךְ בְּ = to pull at, tug: מָשַׁךְ בַּחֶבֶל. Without בְּ, מָשַׁךְ + object = to pull something along, or to attract: זֶה מוֹשֵׁךְ אוֹתִי (it attracts me). בַּשָּׁלָב הַזֶּה = at this point.

w: עַד כְּדֵי כָּךְ שֶׁ|so much that|~fixed phrase
s.line: and this made it so much lighter in weight than the air without that it pulled hard to rise into the sky.
s.note: עַד כְּדֵי כָּךְ שֶׁ = "to such an extent that", the "so … that" of English: הוּא הָיָה עָיֵף עַד כְּדֵי כָּךְ שֶׁנִּרְדַּם (he was so tired that he fell asleep). The comparative is קַל … מִ, "light from", with בְּהַרְבֵּה for "much".

s.line: “Come, Dorothy!” cried the Wizard.
“Hurry up, or the balloon will fly away.”
s.note: תְּמַהֲרִי is really a future form ("you will hurry"), but spoken Hebrew uses the future as the normal imperative: תָּבוֹא, תַּגִּידִי, תְּמַהֵר. The textbook imperative מַהֲרִי sounds bookish or very sharp. אַחֶרֶת = otherwise, or else.

s.line: “I can’t find Toto anywhere,” replied Dorothy, who did not wish to leave her little dog behind.
s.note: נִשְׁאַר (nif'al) = to stay, remain; הִשְׁאִיר (hif'il) = to leave something or someone behind, literally "to make stay": הִשְׁאַרְתִּי אֶת הַמַּפְתְּחוֹת בַּבַּיִת. Hebrew says "I don't find" (לֹא מוֹצֵאת) where English says "I can't find".

s.line: Toto had run into the crowd to bark at a kitten, and Dorothy at last found him.
s.note: נָבַח עַל = to bark at. חֲתַלְתּוּל = a kitten, from חָתוּל (cat); a puppy is גּוּר.

s.line: She picked him up and ran towards the balloon.
s.note: רָצָה here is "she ran" (from רָץ, root ר־ו־ץ). Without vowels it looks exactly like רָצָה "he wanted" (root ר־צ־ה): only the context tells you. הֵרִים = to lift, raise; רָם = high.

s.line: She was within a few steps of it, and Oz was holding out his hands to help her into the basket,
s.note: הוֹשִׁיט = to hold out, reach out (a hand); לְהוֹשִׁיט יַד עֶזְרָה = to lend a helping hand. Hebrew uses הַיָּדַיִם ("the hands") where English says "his hands".

s.line: when, crack! went the ropes, and the balloon rose into the air without her.
s.note: נִקְרַע = was torn, ripped (nif'al of קָרַע, to tear). בִּלְעָדֶיהָ = without her: בְּלִי takes endings through the form בִּלְעֲדֵי: בִּלְעָדַי (without me), בִּלְעָדֶיךָ, בִּלְעָדָיו. In casual speech you also hear בְּלִי אוֹתָהּ.

s.line: “Come back!” she screamed.
“I want to go, too!”
“I can’t come back, my dear,” called Oz from the basket.
“Good-bye!”
s.note: שָׁלוֹם is both "hello" and "goodbye". For a parting you also hear לְהִתְרָאוֹת (see you), a hitpa'el of רָאָה: "to see each other", and the borrowed בַּיי.

s.line: “Good-bye!” shouted everyone,

w: יוֹתֵר וְיוֹתֵר|and higher|~lit. more and more
s.line: and all eyes were turned upward to where the Wizard was riding in the basket, rising every moment farther and farther into the sky.
s.note: מֻפְנֶה is the hof'al (passive) participle of הִפְנָה (hif'il, to turn something toward, to direct): "turned, directed". הִפְנָה אוֹתִי לְרוֹפֵא = he referred me to a doctor. X יוֹתֵר וְיוֹתֵר = more and more X: קַר יוֹתֵר וְיוֹתֵר (colder and colder).

s.line: And that was the last any of them ever saw of Oz, the Wonderful Wizard,
though he may have reached Omaha safely, and be there now, for all we know.
s.note: יִתָּכֵן = "it is possible, perhaps", a higher-register word you will meet in the news: יִתָּכֵן שֶׁיֵּרֵד גֶּשֶׁם (it may rain). Its opposite, לֹא יִתָּכֵן!, = "that can't be!", "that's unacceptable!" בְּשָׁלוֹם = safely, in one piece.

w: זֶה לָזֶה|to one another|~lit. this to this
s.line: But the people remembered him lovingly, and said to one another:
s.note: זֶה לָזֶה = to one another; about women זוֹ לָזוֹ. Modern speech often uses אֶחָד לַשֵּׁנִי instead.

s.line: “Oz was always our friend.
When he was here he built for us this beautiful Emerald City,
s.note: In עִיר הָאִזְמָרַגְד הַיָּפָה הַזֹּאת the adjectives come after the whole construct phrase and agree with its first noun, עִיר (feminine), not with אִזְמָרַגְד. That is why it is הַיָּפָה and הַזֹּאת.

s.line: and now he is gone he has left the Wise Scarecrow to rule over us.”
Still, for many days they grieved over the loss of the Wonderful Wizard, and would not be comforted.
s.note: לֹא הִסְכִּימוּ לְהִתְנַחֵם = "would not be comforted". Baum's phrase echoes the Bible, where Jacob mourns Joseph and מֵאֵן לְהִתְנַחֵם (refused to be comforted). נִחֵם (pi'el) = to comfort; הִתְנַחֵם (hitpa'el) = to be comforted, console oneself. הִתְאַבֵּל = to mourn; אֵבֶל = mourning.
